title: Food banks
hookLine: langar's spirit in a food bank
tomorrow: kiran's mom wants company. what do you say to someone sick?

cards: Saturday, a church basement that smells of cardboard and coffee. Maya's grandma runs the canned-goods table at the food bank here, and Simran and Maya are sorting beans by date.
Taped above the shelves is a verse from Matthew: For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat. Simran tells her about langar, the free kitchen where anyone can sit and eat. Maya's grandma smiles.
So this is langar too? Simran opens her mouth, and isn't sure.

teach.h: ONE SIDE: LANGAR IS THE PANGAT.
teach.b: It's a real question, and Sikhs answer it two ways. One side says: careful. Langar isn't only free food.
Tradition says Guru Amar Das asked everyone who came to see him to eat in the pangat first: sitting in rows on the floor, the same food, side by side, whoever they were.
The heart of langar is that equality, nobody served above anybody. A box handed across a table, however kind, isn't quite that.
The other side says: the heart of langar is that nobody goes hungry. The Guru's kitchen fed whoever came, and the people in a food-bank line are hungry today.

A Sikh who carries that into a church basement or a school pantry is carrying langar's spirit. Here's the fair way to hold it. The first view protects something precious that's easy to lose: sitting together.
The second protects something urgent: the hungry person in front of you.
Some Sikhs keep both: the pangat at the gurdwara, and its spirit out the door.
And what's shared with Maya's grandma's verse? In Matthew, Jesus says that feeding the hungry is done to him.
Langar feeds the hungry with no one ranked above anyone. Two different reasons, the same full plate.

how: Gurdwaras serve langar to anyone who comes, seated in the pangat; Sikh volunteers also cook for shelters and give to food banks in their towns.

s: it's the shared meal in the pangat, where everyone sits as equals.
tradition says Guru Amar Das asked visitors to eat in the pangat first
same food, same floor, whoever they were.
Matthew's 'I was an hungred' and langar are the same idea
they share feeding the hungry; Matthew's frame is doing it to Jesus, langar's is equality at the meal.

games.q: your cousin says a food bank isn't langar, because nobody sits together as equals. what's the best case for her side?
o: langar's heart is the pangat: same food, same floor, nobody above anybody.
food banks are run by other faiths, so they can never be langar.
langar has to be cooked by Sikhs, or it doesn't count at all.
games.why: the pangat view protects sitting together as equals, which a handout can lose. the other view protects the hungry person today. some Sikhs keep both.

practice: If there's something to eat near you, bread, a cracker, a piece of fruit, hold it a moment and smell it. Take one slow bite, and taste it as the same food someone in a pangat, or a food-bank line, might be eating right now.
Then rest your hands and sit.

wordCard.voice: Food banks. Places that give food to whoever is hungry; langar's spirit outside the gurdwara. Pangat: the rows where all sit as equals.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: langar, the Guru's free kitchen and shared meal, open to all.

carryVoice: Your line: langar everywhere. The rows stay at the gurdwara; the spirit travels. See you soon.
